checkpoints: A single classify(event, watermark) function sits at the boundary, and the rest of the pipeline depends only on its return value
The output is an explicit status (accepted / late / fraud) plus evidence like lateMs and reason, not a bare true/false
Lateness is decided by comparing the event's eventTime against watermark minus a tolerance
Only accepted events are allowed to advance the watermark, keeping it monotonic so a late event can never reopen a closed window
A late verdict can be merged back into its correct window if it's still within a grace period
A late verdict can instead be side-outputted to a separate path for later batch reprocessing with wider tolerance (lambda/kappa pattern) once past the grace period
A late verdict is discarded outright only when the business has explicitly decided stale data past some point is worthless — never as a silent, undocumented drop

Because the underlying Kafka log is append-only, every click — accepted, late, or fraud — stays retained regardless of its classification, so a flagged-late click can still be recovered later, unlike one silently dropped
One table, ad_click_counts(adId, windowStart, count), on the ReplacingMergeTree engine

ORDER BY (adId, windowStart) is itself the replacement key: rows sharing that key get merged down to the last-inserted one, so re-flushing a window under at-least-once delivery replaces rather than double-counts
The (adId, windowStart) row is the finest grain the table stores and is the single source of truth; every report is just a different view over it
The 'clicks per minute per ad' report is GROUP BY adId, windowStart — the same grain, no rollup
The 'total clicks per ad' report is GROUP BY adId only, dropping windowStart to roll up to a coarser grain on the same table, with no second table needed
One roll-up table beats a separate table per report because dual writes can drift apart on partial failure, whereas one table lets a new report be just another GROUP BY with no new write path
The table's finest grain (the minute) can't answer sub-minute questions like a specific click at second 34 — that requires going back to raw events in Kafka
Because ReplacingMergeTree merges asynchronously, reads must use FINAL or argMax(count, version) to avoid summing un-merged duplicate versions
Every click carries a stable idempotency key, clickId, that stays the same across retries
clickId is supplied by the client per real tap, or minted as a UUID by the API only when the field is missing
The consumer keeps a seen-index — durable dedup state — of every clickId it has already counted
For each incoming record the consumer checks seen FIRST: if the clickId is already there, it bumps a duplicate tally and returns without touching the count
Only if the clickId is new does the consumer add it to seen and increment that adId's count by one

This check-before-increment order guarantees exactly one clickId can ever raise the count no matter how many times Kafka redelivers it (client retry, rebalance, or restart), turning at-least-once delivery into count-once processing
The seen-index itself must live in durable, eventually bounded storage (e.g. TTL'd or external store), since a plain in-memory set would be lost on crash and grow unbounded
The pipeline is not "add a time column and GROUP BY when needed" — it's compressing the stream into per-window counts as it flows by.

Every click carries an eventTime; flooring that eventTime to the minute boundary produces a windowStart, so every click within the same minute falls into exactly one tumbling window (adjacent, non-overlapping).
The counting key is the pair (adId, windowStart): instead of writing one row per click, the aggregator keeps an in-memory Map and just +1s the right cell for that pair.
The number of cells scales with the number of ads times the number of open minutes, not with click volume at all.
Periodically (e.g. every 10 seconds), all accumulated cells are gathered into one batch and inserted in a single call, instead of writing a row per click continuously.
That batch lands in ClickHouse — a columnar store built to scan/aggregate fast over large row counts and one that strongly prefers large batched inserts over a constant stream of tiny ones.

The result is a roll-up table (adId, windowStart, count) orders of magnitude smaller than the raw click table, so the "clicks per minute per ad" report becomes a cheap SELECT ... GROUP BY windowStart over that table instead of a full scan of billions of raw rows every time.

The trade-off is that once compressed into counts, per-click detail is gone — to investigate a specific click later (e.g. a suspected fraud case), you have to go back to the raw log still held in Kafka, since it can't be recovered from the roll-up table.
Keying by adId is the right call when per-ad ordering still matters, but it isn't free.
Because Kafka hashes the key to pick a partition, the same adId always lands on the same partition, preserving the relative order between that ad's clicks.

That ordering is exactly the foundation the downstream windowed-aggregation layer relies on: grouping and counting per ad happens neatly inside one partition, with no need to merge data across partitions.

The cost shows up when one ad goes viral: its huge volume of clicks still all funnel into the one partition it hashed to from the start, turning that partition into a hotspot whose consumer carries far more load than the others and caps the parallelism of the whole pipeline no matter how many consumers are added to the group.
Deliberately stop keying by adId when strict per-ad ordering isn't actually a business requirement (only the correct total matters, not the correct sequence).
Or when you know in advance a few ads will dominate traffic — add a sub-key like adId|bucket_n (hashing in a small random or round-robin number) to spread one ad's clicks across several partitions.
Sum the buckets back together on read to get the correct total, trading strict intra-ad ordering for load balance.

Partition count isn't something you can freely increase later — raising it changes how adId maps to a partition and can break the relative order of clicks already written before the reshard, so size the partition count for expected parallelism from the start.

A tumbling window slices the time axis into adjacent, non-overlapping, equal-width intervals; flooring eventTime to the window boundary puts every click in exactly one window — the same mechanism this lesson's aggregator uses to bucket clicks into (adId, windowStart).
That's why tumbling is the right shape for "clicks per minute": each bar is an independent, self-contained total — nothing double-counted, nothing missing.

A sliding (hopping) window instead overlaps: a 5-minute window that advances every 1 minute has its boundary move every minute while its width stays 5 minutes, so one click's eventTime lands inside several currently-open windows simultaneously.

That overlapping shape is what "5-minute moving average, updated every minute" needs, since the metric must keep re-expressing "the last 5 minutes" every minute rather than produce five separate self-contained totals.

The per-minute bar chart stays tumbling and the moving average becomes sliding — they answer different questions ("how many in this exact slice" vs "how many over the trailing N slices"), and forcing one window model to serve both would either break the bar chart's independence or under-smooth the average.

The catch is cost: because a sliding window overlaps, a single click's count update has to fan out to every currently-open window it falls inside — with a 5x overlap factor (5-minute window, 1-minute hop) that is roughly 5 live buckets touched per click instead of 1.

Both the number of concurrently open windows kept in memory and the per-event work scale with the overlap factor — a deliberate trade a senior engineer states out loud, not something the tumbling aggregator gives for free.

A watermark advances to the maximum eventTime seen and promises no event will arrive with an eventTime below watermark - tolerance; the tolerance is exactly how much out-of-orderness you're willing to absorb before calling an event late.

Widening the tolerance to 5 minutes admits far more late events into their correct window (more complete), but costs added latency — every window now waits up to 5 minutes past its own boundary before it can be considered "done".
Widening also costs more memory, since per-window counters and seen-state sit around longer before being evicted.
Shrinking the tolerance to 2 seconds closes windows almost immediately (low latency, tiny memory footprint).

But shrinking wrongly flags genuinely in-flight events as late, dropping them from their true window or shunting them into a correction path, undercounting real numbers just because the network was briefly slow.
Neither direction is "more correct" in isolation — it's a dial between completeness and latency, and the right setting depends entirely on how out-of-order the real traffic actually is.

The watermark itself is never allowed to move backward, only advancing to the max eventTime observed; if it retreated to accommodate one especially old straggler, every window that had already closed between the old and new watermark position would effectively reopen, breaking a downstream consumer's already-reported "window X is final" and risking endless oscillation instead of a stable answer.

In practice you pick the tolerance empirically — measure the actual out-of-orderness distribution of production traffic (how late 95-99% of events really arrive), set the tolerance to comfortably cover that common case, and route the small tail of pathologically late events to a side output or batch reprocessing job instead of blowing up the tolerance for everyone.

Kafka commits and tracks consumed offsets per consumer group, not per process or container instance - a restart of the same physical service instance is invisible to Kafka unless the group identity changes.
Calling `randomUUID()` inside the consumer bootstrap mints a brand-new, never-before-seen `groupId` on every process start, so Kafka has no committed offset on record for that group name.

`subscribe: { fromBeginning: true }` is only meant to apply on a consumer group's true first-ever run; when the `groupId` itself is regenerated on every boot, every restart looks like a first run, so the flag fires again and again.

The combination of a fresh `groupId` plus `fromBeginning: true` causes the entire `ad-clicks` topic to be replayed from offset 0 on every restart, streaming every historical `clickId` through the consumer a second time.

The minimal fix is to pin a fixed, stable `groupId` (e.g. via config or an env var) that stays constant across restarts, so Kafka returns the group's last committed offset and the consumer resumes from where it left off instead of from the beginning.

Even with a stable `groupId`, a dedup `seen` set kept only in memory is wiped on every restart, so if Kafka redelivers a record under its at-least-once guarantee around a crash, the consumer can no longer recognize it as a duplicate.

Correct production behavior requires the dedup index to live in a durable store (such as Redis or RocksDB) alongside a stable `groupId`, since offset management alone does not guarantee exactly-once processing.

The fix can be verified by restarting the consumer with no new clicks sent and confirming `GET /counts` stays exactly flat, then sending one new click and confirming only that single click is added to the count.
A watermark is a monotonic high-water mark: a standing promise that no event will arrive earlier than `watermark - tolerance`, so it must only ever move forward in time, never backward.

In the given code, `this.watermarkMs = eventMs` runs unconditionally at the very top of `process()`, before the late-check even executes, with no guard comparing the incoming event time against the current watermark.

Because the assignment is unconditional, a back-dated event (for example one arriving two minutes in the past) drags `watermarkMs` down to its own older timestamp, dragging the watermark backward instead of leaving it at the highest event time actually seen.

Once the watermark has retreated into the past, the very next on-time event is compared against that artificially low value in `eventMs < this.watermarkMs - this.watermarkToleranceMs`, so the condition is far less likely to trip and events that are genuinely late relative to the stream's true progress start sailing through as `accepted`.

This effectively reopens a window the true watermark had already closed, and the resulting accepted/late classification becomes unstable and dependent on the exact order in which events happen to be interleaved, rather than on each event's own timestamp.

The fix is to make the watermark update conditional and move it after the late-check: only assign `this.watermarkMs = eventMs` when `eventMs > this.watermarkMs`, inside the branch that already determined the event is not late, so a late event is still classified `late` but never gets to move the watermark.

Correct behaviour can be verified by replaying an on-time -> late -> on-time sequence and asserting that the watermark value never decreases step to step, the back-dated click is reported as `late`, and the on-time clicks that follow it remain `accepted` rather than flipping to `late`.

A MergeTree table ordered by (adId, windowStart) never deduplicates on that key at write time — it simply appends every inserted row, so two flushes of the same window leave two separate rows sitting side by side in the table.

Kafka's at-least-once delivery means a message can be redelivered after a crash, so an aggregator that restarts mid-window will, under normal operation, re-flush the same (adId, windowStart) bucket a second time.

A read query using sum(count) GROUP BY adId, windowStart is only correct when each key has been written exactly once; once a duplicate row exists for that key, the same sum() silently adds both rows together and doubles the reported click count.

ClickHouse has no cheap row-level UPDATE, so making the flush idempotent has to be solved at the storage-engine level rather than by adding existence checks or conditional logic to the application's flush code.

Swapping ENGINE = MergeTree for ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree() while keeping the same ORDER BY (adId, windowStart) turns that ordering key into a replacement key, so a later background merge keeps only the most recently inserted row per key instead of accumulating every version.

ReplacingMergeTree's deduplication happens during asynchronous background merges, not at insert time, so a plain SELECT run immediately after a re-flush can still return multiple un-merged rows for the same key.

Because merge timing isn't guaranteed, a report reading from a ReplacingMergeTree table must use FINAL or an aggregate like argMax(count, version) GROUP BY key instead of sum(count) — this forces the deduplicated, latest-per-key value even when the background merge hasn't run yet.

Idempotency under redelivery is verified by flushing the same window twice in a row to simulate a crash-and-replay, then asserting the FINAL/argMax read returns the single latest count rather than the sum of both flushes.
